score_meanings.app_protocol_promise_semantics: 0 uses command/permission framing, 5 models storage, computation, send/receive, reciprocal promises, local trust, and make/break evidence
score_meanings.envelope_discipline: 0 ignores the settled envelope direction or confuses pCID, 5 aligns with grid([42(pCID), payload, ...]), Protocol-CID semantics, and protocol-owned later slots
score_meanings.kernel_implementation_promises: 0 treats the kernel as authority or generic port conformance, 5 names local kernel implementation promises, assumptions, unsupported behavior, and evidence
score_meanings.promise_vocabulary: 0 drifts into claims/profiles/generic statement capsules/central trust-ledger framing, 5 stays promise-first, layer-local, and pCID-specific
score_meanings.simplicity_durability: 0 overbuilt, selector-shopping, or fragile, 5 minimal, durable, and small-device-friendly under the 100-year goal

promise_theory_rules: A promise is a scoped declaration of intent.
No agent can make a promise on behalf of another agent.
Trust is a local assessment of whether a promise will be kept.
Promises to receive or use are not equivalent to obligations, impositions, or promises to give.
promise_theory_references: Mark Burgess, In Search of Certainty
Mark Burgess, Promise Theory: Principles and Applications

assessment.rationale: Strong as a PromiseGrid-oriented question home for kernel/runtime boundary setting, but weak as a scored solution to the scenario because it intentionally stops short of a concrete porting target, explicit kernel promise record, refusal/evidence mechanics, or envelope-level implementation detail.
strengths: Explicitly frames the work as provisional and boundary-setting rather than falsely settled API guidance.
Focuses attention on minimum viable port, layer boundaries, and separation of harness apparatus from real implementation target.
Compatible with Promise Theory because it avoids authority claims and leaves promisers/host assumptions to be made explicit later.
weaknesses: Does not provide the actual first porting plan or kernel implementation promise record demanded by the scenario.
Does not specify concrete pCID-selected message handling, refusal behavior, exact-byte evidence retention, or unsupported-role treatment.
Provides little direct envelope, app-protocol, or kernel-promise vocabulary beyond the open questions.
risks: Developers may still mistake the wire-lab harness or one runtime shape for the actual porting target.
The term "kernel" may harden prematurely before the real runtime boundary is frozen.
Lack of concrete mandatory promise-record fields may produce inconsistent ports and weak audit evidence.
open_questions: Should the guide keep the term "kernel" or switch to "runtime" or a narrower dispatcher/handler-host term?
What minimum frozen pCID/spec set defines a credible first port before DR-davod closes?
Which host assumptions, unsupported pCIDs, refusal forms, and exact-byte evidence obligations must be mandatory in a first implementation promise record?
assessment.authority_boundary: Evidence only; does not settle PromiseGrid design.

autonomous_agents.note: The sim does not deny agent autonomy and leaves promisers/hosts as separate actors to be named later.

scoped_intent.note: The document is scoped as a provisional question home about the porting boundary, not a universal settled design.

no_promises_for_others.note: The sim does not make promises on behalf of browsers, hosts, or other services; it explicitly questions that boundary.

no_guaranteed_outcomes.note: No guaranteed delivery or success semantics are claimed.

local_trust_assessment.note: It does not rely on global trust; trust and implementation claims remain local and provisional.

accept_use_not_obligation.note: No obligation or command framing is asserted; the sim stays at the level of optional implementation boundary questions.
